messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Lin, a 76-year-old South Eastern Asian man and former warehouse worker, has struggled with the aftermath of his experiences in a war zone for years. Living alone, he often finds himself grappling with vivid memories that feel as fresh and terrifying today as they did decades ago. One particular incident from his past stands out vividly: during an air raid, Mr. Lin was trapped under debris while the sounds of explosions echoed around him. The smell of smoke filled the air, and he felt a sense of suffocation as he lay immobilized, waiting for rescue. This experience has left him with specific triggers that activate powerful memories without warning. At work in the warehouse, the scent of burning wood or diesel fumes can instantly transport Mr. Lin back to those harrowing moments. The smell itself is often enough to trigger a vivid and overwhelming recall of the air raid. Once this memory surfaces, he finds himself completely overwhelmed by the emotions it brings forth, forcing him to pause his work until the intensity subsides. One day at the warehouse, while handling boxes near machinery with diesel fumes, Mr. Lin suddenly felt as if he were back in that moment under debris. The smell of diesel triggered an immediate and vivid recollection of the air raid, and he had to stop what he was doing. This cycle often disrupts his work routine, making it difficult for him to focus on tasks. These triggers are not limited to olfactory stimuli; tactile sensations also play a significant role in activating his memories. When Mr. Lin is physically restrained or held down during a medical examination or even accidentally bumped into by someone walking past, the sensation can quickly bring back those frightening moments of feeling trapped and immobilized. These instances reinforce his belief that any form of physical restraint could lead to a similar feeling of helplessness. Mr. Lin’s fear of confrontation also stems from these experiences. He recalls the intense tension during skirmishes in the war zone, where conflict was a constant threat. This has made him wary of any situation that might involve disagreement or hostility. His memories are so vivid and detailed that even minor confrontations can evoke powerful feelings of dread, making it difficult for him to engage with others without experiencing overwhelming anxiety. Mr. Lin’s memory quality adds another layer to his distress. The clarity and detail of these recollections ensure that they are not just fleeting thoughts but full-fledged experiences that leave a lasting impact on his daily life. When he remembers the air raid, every detail is etched into his mind—every sound, every smell, every sensation—leaving him feeling as if he were reliving it in real time. This cycle of triggers and memories has significantly affected Mr. Lin’s ability to function normally. His work performance has suffered due to frequent disruptions caused by these intrusive recollections, and his relationships have been strained because of his avoidance of potentially triggering situations. What finally brought Mr. Lin to seek help was a combination of increasing isolation and the realization that he could no longer manage on his own. He is most afraid of feeling trapped or helpless again, but he also hopes for relief from these overwhelming memories and triggers. Seeking professional support, Mr. Lin is looking for ways to regain control over his life and find peace with his past experiences.
